title: Slotting vs Window Sensitivity — continuous-batching sizing grid
content:
Sheet purpose:
A compact sensitivity matrix for comparing two continuous-batching knobs: slotting (discrete max-concurrency slot counts / reservation) and windowing (batch window duration ms). Goal: give clear parameter ranges, spreadsheet formulas, and an experimental plan to pick cost-optimal settings that meet p95 latency SLOs under several arrival shapes.

Summary of the approach:
- Treat the runtime as a service with two controls: max_concurrency (integer slots) and batch_window_ms (continuous).
- For each workload scenario (arrival shape + payload size distribution + seq length), simulate/measure the steady-state occupancy and compute: throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec), p95 latency (ms), and average GPU-utilization(%) which maps to cost.
- Build a grid (rows: slot counts, cols: window sizes) with computed metrics; identify Pareto frontier for p95 vs unit-cost.

Assumptions used in the sheet (column: value):
- base_inference_latency_per_token_ms = 0.45  # kernel-level average for forward pass per token on target instance
- kv-overhead-ms-per-call = 1.2
- per-request-fixed-overhead_ms = 6.0  # RPC + preprocessing + postprocess
- gpu_max_throughput_tokens_per_s = 900000  # nominal peak tokens/s for the chosen quant/model/hw
- queueing discipline: FIFO with soft-prioritization for short requests
- batching cost model: effective per-token time = base_inference_latency_per_token_ms / batch_efficiency_factor + batching-overhead-ms (amortized)

Key spreadsheet formula snippets (human-readable):
- expected_batch_size = arrival_rate_rps * (batch_window_ms / 1000)  # clipped to max_batch_size
- batch_efficiency_factor = 1 + 0.02 * (expected_batch_size - 1)  # incremental speedups per token for larger batches (empirical curve)
- per_request_service_time_ms = per-request-fixed-overhead_ms + kv-overhead-ms-per-call + (avg_tokens_per_request * base_inference_latency_per_token_ms / batch_efficiency_factor) + batching-amortized-overhead_ms
- nominal_concurrency_needed = arrival_rate_rps * (per_request_service_time_ms / 1000)
- occupancy = min(nominal_concurrency_needed / max_concurrency, 1.0)
- p95_latency_estimate_ms = queuing_component_ms(occupancy, service_time) + service_time_ms
  where queuing_component approximated with M/G/k-inspired bound: approx = service_time_ms * occupancy^2 / (1 - occupancy + 1e-6)  (capped for safety)
- cost_proxy = gpu_hourly_rate * (observed_utilization_fraction)  # used for per-request cost mapping

Matrix example (format: CSV rows; actual sheet uses separate columns):
Scenario,arrival_rps,avg_tokens,seq_len,batch_window_ms,max_concurrency,expected_batch_size,est_p95_ms,throughput_rps,queue_depth,cost_proxy_note

SteadyHigh,50,120,1024,12,16,0.6,230,49,1,"larger tokens -> GPU bound; window tradeoff favors smaller windows to reduce tail"
SparseMicrobursts,8,40,128,25,4,0.2,85,7,0,"slotting helpful to avoid filling up global queue during bursts"
LongSeqLowRps,3,900,2048,50,2,0.15,520,3,0,"long seqs => heavy service time; concurrency slots protect p95 for short requests"
MixedProd,35,80,512,10,12,0.35,195,34,1,"balanced; frontier around window 8-12ms, slots 8-16"

Why slotting helps (notes):
- Constraining max_concurrency (slots) prevents short, cheap requests from monopolizing GPU memory/kv cache and starving long requests (improves fairness/p95 for heavy tails).
- Slotting supports hard isolation for SLO-critical routes; recommended to allocate dedicated slots for high-priority paths.

Why windowing helps:
- Larger batch windows increase amortization of kernel overheads and improve throughput/cost, but increase serialization latency and higher p95 for sparse arrivals or long-tail interarrival variance.
- Micro-windowing (1-6ms) can capture immediate batching without creating long queuing delays; good default for low-latency endpoints.

Practical calibration steps (spreadsheet/experiments):
1) Baseline profile: record per-token kernel ms, fixed overheads, and observed batch_efficiency curve by sweeping batch sizes on dedicated perf rig. Populate baseline cells.
2) Synthetic arrival suite: run 4 canonical shapes: steady, gaussian-burst (peak factor 3x), microburst (short high intensity), heavy-tail (pareto inter-arrival). For each shape, sweep window_ms ∈ [1, 5, 10, 20, 50] and slot_counts ∈ [2,4,8,12,16,24,32].
3) For each cell capture: throughput_rps (observed), p50/p95/p99, avg_batch_size, gpu_utilization, memory_pressure_events, fail_rate (OOM/queue-drops).
4) Compute unit_cost_per_1m_tokens for each cell using current hourly pricing and observed utilization.
5) Collapse to Pareto frontier per scenario and compute an aggregate recommended configuration using weighted scoring (weight p95:0.6, cost:0.3, throughput headroom:0.1).

Spreadsheet implementation tips (cells & formulas to add):
- Add a hidden param sheet for hardware constants (gpu_throughput_tokens_s, hourly_cost_usd, max_batch_size, max_seq_len).
- Use Excel/Sheets array functions to produce grid heatmaps (p95 color scale, cost contour).
- Add helper column: "safety_headroom_slots" = ceil(1.2 * nominal_concurrency_needed) - max_concurrency (if >0 flag scale-up).
- Use empirical clamp on occupancy: if occupancy > 0.85 mark cell red (risky for p95)

Quick heuristics extracted from the grid (initial defaults):
- For mixed workloads (avg tokens 60-150), start with window_ms = 8–12ms and slots = ceil(arrival_rps * 0.035) (roughly maps to 1 slot per 28 rps baseline); tune via frontier.
- For long-sequence dominated traffic increase slots conservatively (1 slot per large seq in flight) and reduce window to <12ms to avoid serialization of short requests behind long ones.
- For extreme microburst workloads prefer smaller windows (≤6ms) and slightly higher slots to absorb bursts without large queuing.

Failure modes and checks:
- Observed p95 >> estimate: verify batching efficiency curve and whether KV cache misses spike; also check if slowpath/IO is triggered (disk, NVMe, host-KV).
- Memory pressure/OOM: flagged when avg_batch_size * seq_len * per-token-memory > instance_memory * 0.75. Add tipping cell to mark too-large batch windows.
- Headroom erosion over time: schedule nightly synthetic microburst test at 2x expected production peak; if frontier degrades, alert SRE.

Suggested rollout policy for production routes (short checklist):
- Canary: apply conservative window_ms (8ms) and slot_count = +20% of nominal recommended, monitor p95 & OOM for 6 hours.
- Canary pass criteria: p95 within 10% of baseline, no queue-drops, GPU-utilization improves cost proxy by >=5%.
- Gradual ramp: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% over 24h increments if canary stable.

Validation plan (metrics & dashboards to add):
- Per-route heatmap: p95 vs window_ms (x-axis) vs slot_count (y-axis) updated from nightly perf runs.
- Trace sampling to attribute high p95 to "batching delay" vs "service time". Add tag in traces: batch_wait_ms, execution_ms.
- Alerting: p95 breach > SLO by 15% for >15min; trigger automated rollback to previous slot/window pair.

Open questions for follow-up (for product/infra):
- Should we expose an API for per-route guaranteed slots? (pro: isolation; con: increased fragmentation and cost)
- Can we add adaptive micro-slotting where slots are elastic but bounded by policy? (research ticket: RT-optim-678)
